release_focus: Fixed two-query joint-precision boundary and exact assurance feasibility.
title: Risk and Adaptivity in Certifying Machine-Learning Model Comparisons
abstract:
Background. Model audits often share a limited set of verification readings across several predictors. We ask whether sharing this budget changes the value of choosing later readings after seeing earlier answers.

Methods. We study sharp intervals for affine model-loss contrasts on compact convex sets using a fixed finite query dictionary. We prove fixed-budget bounds, supply exact certificates, and replay two-reading policies on cumulative-meter data.

Results. For one comparison, if a deterministic policy guarantees precision with two exact scalar readings, some randomized fixed batch succeeds with worst-case probability at least 1/2. This lower bound disappears with two comparisons. For every m>=3, we construct instances where adaptation always succeeds but the best randomized batch succeeds with worst-case probability exactly 1/m. All coordinates are queryable, the budget remains two, and each comparison is separately certifiable by a fixed batch. The separation also holds for all pairwise comparisons among three models. In the meter application, 165 of 819 original blocks and 57 of 279 external blocks have verified adaptive success one versus optimal batch success 1/2. Recorded gains over fixed worst-width batches are 7.81 and 11.11 percentage points; gains over greedy adaptation are 2.20 and 2.15 points. Capacity information reduces the advantage, and measured public-API retrieval favors bulk.

Conclusions. Sharing a reading budget can make feedback necessary for assurance even when separate comparisons need none. The construction proves a fixed-budget boundary; the retrospective meter study establishes its narrower, instance-specific counterpart under declared access rules.
